chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl bin Ziyad and Muhammad bin Yahya, from Ahmad bin Muhammad, all from Ibn Mahboub, from Amr bin Abu al-Miqdam, who said:

I passed by Al-Baqi' cemetery with Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), so we passed by the grave of a man from the people of Kufa from the Shias. He (peace be upon him) paused at it and said: 'O Allah, have mercy on his estrangement, and connect his loneliness, and comfort his solitude, and settle upon him from Your mercy that which makes him independent of the mercy of others besides You, and join him with those who used to be his friends/protectors.'

key_terms.الْبَقِيعُ: Al-Baqi', a famous cemetery in Medina
key_terms.الْغُرْبَةُ: Estrangement or being a stranger, referring to the soul's state in the grave
key_terms.يَتَوَلَّاهُ: He befriended him / He was his guardian or close companion

ai.seo_question: What is the supplication for the deceased regarding loneliness and mercy in the grave?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi highlights the Shia practice of visiting graves (Ziyarat) with a focus on the spiritual state of the deceased, specifically addressing the 'ghurba' (estrangement) and 'wahsha' (loneliness) experienced in the grave. The supplication reflects the theological emphasis on divine self-sufficiency (ghina) and the communal bond of the Shia, asking Allah to reunite the deceased with his spiritual companions. It underscores the intercessory role of the Imam and the belief that the mercy of Allah is sufficient to render the deceased independent of other creatures' mercy.
